visual_accuracy.rationale: Lesson 1 consistently shows the correct projectile setup, component vectors at a plausible 30° angle, flight path, landing point, and final range marker, whereas Lesson 2’s launch vector/component diagram is visually too steep/misaligned for 30° and later leaves sustained unrelated/faded quiz/formula artifacts that obscure the intended solution visuals.

interactivity.rationale: Both lessons include a real wired fill-in gate after act_decomposition, but Lesson 2 is slightly more functional as an interactive check because its prompt is more self-contained with supplied trig approximations and multiple accepted answer formats, while Lesson 1 relies on rounding to a single exact accepted string and has the same plan/spec mismatch about asking for both components versus only one.

narration_quality.rationale: Lesson 2 sounds slightly more natural and conversational with clearer spoken math like “v-naught-x,” while Lesson 1 is also clear but has somewhat more awkward phrasing such as “v-zero-x” and a less smooth explanatory flow.

sync.rationale: Lesson 1’s cues generally appear when the narration introduces the corresponding vector, trajectory, equations, and focus shifts, whereas Lesson 2 has several poorly timed or missing visual changes, such as decomposing well before it is mentioned and referencing equations, substitutions, and numeric results without synchronized cues.

concept_accuracy.rationale: Lesson 1 is more conceptually accurate and pedagogically clear because it explicitly decomposes velocity, solves the vertical kinematics equation for flight time, computes the horizontal range, and derives the range formula, whereas Lesson 2 mostly asserts these steps without showing the equations/calculations and even ends with the misleading phrase that the motion splits into “two simple linear motions” despite vertical motion being accelerated.

polish.rationale: Lesson 1 maintains a more coherent, legible split-screen layout with consistent styling despite some cramped/cropped right-panel content, while Lesson 2 has visible player controls, raw backtick-style notation, excessive empty space, dim/faded elements lingering, and a less polished off-center composition.

aggregator.explanation: Lesson 1 is the clear overall winner: four of six agents favored it, and those wins were all high-confidence, especially for concept accuracy, synchronization, visual accuracy, and polish. Lesson 2 had modest advantages in interactivity and narration, but both were lower-confidence and relatively slight. The strongest factors favor Lesson 1 because it more accurately presents the projectile setup, better synchronizes visuals with narration, explicitly shows the kinematics reasoning, and maintains a cleaner, more coherent visual layout.
